newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zaire force general admits differences with Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Zaire force general admits differences with Rwanda.

text.p: The leader of a planned intervention force for eastern Zaire left Rwanda on Tuesday acknowledging differences existed between the United Nations and the Rwandan government on the need for the force.
Canadian Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril was speaking at the end of an assessment mission with U.N. troubleshooter Raymond Chretien during which they met Rwandan Vice-President Paul Kagame.
"There is a different opinion (between us and the Rwandan government) and that is why I am here. I am really trying to clarify what is going on," Baril told reporters.
Rwanda earlier said there was no need for a military intervention force now since almost all the Rwandan Hutu refugees had returned home.

"They (Rwanda) feel that most of the problem has been solved and therefore they don't see any need for the same kind of military mission as envisaged a week ago, so that's clearly their position," Chretien said.

"We have to know what is happening on the other side (of the border). There are still approximately between 300,000-500,000 according to our best estimates and we have to know a bit more about what is happening to them," he said.
Resolving those differences in part depended on a precise assessment of the refugee situation in eastern Zaire.
Baril was due to go to Uganda and then Stuttgart, Germany, for a meeting with other countries participating in the planned intervention force, while Chretien was bound for Kinshasa.
"No recommendations, no decisions have been made by the troops contributors so far and I haven't put my recommendations in yet," Baril said on the upcoming meeting.
Earlier Rwanda's foreign minister said the force was no longer needed since there were hardly any refugees left in eastern Zaire, contrary to U.N. estimates that well over half a million remained.

"These refugees who have returned home number 500,000 people, which broadly matches the real number of Rwandan refugees previously in eastern Zaire, in North and South Kivu," Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana said in a statement.
"We're not saying that there's not a single refugee in eastern Zaire," Gasana told a news conference. "There could be a few who are tired and can't walk, but the great mass has returned."
Gasana's statistics bore no relation to figures provided by the United Nations and aid agencies.

The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR says there were 1.1 million Rwandan Hutus and 150,000 Burundian Hutus in camps in eastern Zaire before the start of a rebellion by Zairean rebels last month which led to the mass return of Rwandan Hutus.

UNHCR is the source for the estimated 500,000 returning refugees since November 15, but it and aid agencies on the ground say there are hundreds of thousands more Rwandan and Burundian refugees scattered in eastern Zaire.

In his statement Gasana said Hutu refugees thought to be in Zaire's South Kivu province had pushed north because of the fighting and had concentrated in the Mugunga and Lac Vert camps in North Kivu, eventually joining the refugees from those camps in a mass return to Rwanda.
In Paris, Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said there were still 300,000 refugees in Bukavu, 200,000 in Uvira in South Kivu province and 200,000 near Goma in North Kivu.
"The threat of an unprecedented humanitarian disaster remains. We must ensure the security of relief convoys," he said.
